question: Your team uses the agent to write a converter that turns legacy XML build files into a new YAML format. After several rounds, each new version fixes one behavior but breaks another. Engineers only notice these regressions later by checking output by hand. You want each iteration to build reliably on the previous one. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Ask Claude to implement the converter first, then have it generate tests from the finished code so that the suite records the current behavior as correct.
options.reason: The guide puts the test suite before implementation. Tests derived from finished code only lock in its current behavior, including bugs, instead of defining the expected behavior.

options.text: After each manual check, tell Claude that the converter still produces wrong results and ask it to review its own code and fix whatever it finds, without listing specific failures.
options.reason: Vague feedback without specific test failures does not guide progressive improvement. The guide's method is to iterate by sharing concrete test failures from a suite written first.

options.text: Write a test suite covering expected conversions, edge cases, and performance limits before implementation, then iterate by sharing the failing test output with Claude.
options.reason: This is test-driven iteration: the tests are written first and define expected behavior, and the shared failures give Claude specific feedback that guides progressive improvement.

options.text: Rewrite the prose specification in more detail, then ask Claude to regenerate the whole converter from scratch each time a regression is found by hand.
options.reason: Prose descriptions can be interpreted inconsistently, and regenerating from scratch throws away progress. It also gives Claude no concrete test failures to iterate against.
